title: Is Anxiety a Sign of Weak Faith?
excerpt: Jesus told his disciples not to be anxious, and the night before he died he was greatly distressed. Scripture distinguishes the worry that grasps for control from the anxiety that afflicts body and mind, and it has a word for both.
body:
A young mother lies awake most nights running the same list: the cough that might be something, the bill that came in higher than she planned, the look on her husband's face at dinner. She prays about each item, and the list is still running when she finishes, and then a second worry arrives on top of the first, that a woman who really trusted God would be asleep by now. A college student has had three panic attacks this semester, one of them in a chapel service, and a friend told him afterward that "perfect love casts out fear" (1 John 4:18). A deacon who has never missed a Sunday takes a small pill every morning for what his doctor calls generalized anxiety, and he has told no one at church, because he once heard it said from the pulpit that worry is a sin.

The skeptic has watched this and drawn a conclusion. Christianity, he says, tells frightened people that their fear is unbelief, so the anxious believer ends up with two problems instead of one. A faith that cannot tell the difference between a worried mind and a faithless heart, he suspects, never understood either.

He has a point, and the church should hear it before it answers him. The site's page for the person who [can't stop worrying](/help/anxiety) opens with the sentence that the young mother, the student and the deacon most need to hear: "Anxiety doesn't mean your faith is weak. It's a weight on body and soul together, more common in church than anyone lets on, and it needs real care, from God and from people." If the fear has turned into thoughts of not wanting to be alive, don't wait to finish this essay. Call or text 988 now, and use [Find Help](/help) for the other lines. Nothing in what follows is medical advice.

## The Case for Calling It Unbelief

The view that anxiety is a failure of faith is not invented out of nothing, and its most thoughtful holders have serious reasons for it.

Scripture does command it. "Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God" (Philippians 4:6). That is an imperative, and Paul does not soften it. Jesus says the same thing three times in a single passage: "do not be anxious about your life" (Matthew 6:25), "do not be anxious, saying, 'What shall we eat?'" (Matthew 6:31), and "do not be anxious about tomorrow" (Matthew 6:34). In the middle of that teaching he calls his hearers "O you of little faith" (Matthew 6:30). If Jesus links worry to little faith, the argument runs, who are we to unlink them?

There is a pastoral worry behind the argument, too, and it is not a foolish one. Those who hold it fear that if every anxious feeling is renamed a symptom, Christians will lose the ability to repent of the worry that really is sinful: the restless grasping after control, the fretting over money and reputation, the refusal to entrust tomorrow to anyone but ourselves. They fear a church that sends its people to the doctor and stops believing that the gospel has anything to say to a troubled mind.

Some of that has to be granted. A good deal of worry is tangled up with what we trust, and some of it can only be healed by repentance. The man whose whole peace rides on his portfolio will not be cured by breathing exercises. And the Christian who has made anxiety an identity, who uses it to excuse every failure to love, needs to hear that Christ calls him to something better.

But the argument goes wrong when it reads those commands without the rest of Scripture beside them, and especially when it forgets who said them and how they lived.

## What Jesus Was Talking About

The worry Jesus forbids in Matthew 6 comes at the end of a passage about money. He has just said that no one can serve two masters, and that "You cannot serve God and money" (Matthew 6:24). Then comes the word "therefore." The anxiety he addresses is the anxiety of a person whose security rests on what they can hoard, and he answers it by pointing to the birds and the lilies: "Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them" (Matthew 6:26). The Study Bible's note on [Matthew 6](/study/bible/matthew/6) puts it plainly: "Jesus forbids the anxious grasping that tries to secure tomorrow by one's own effort and forgets the Father."

The word itself helps. The Greek verb behind "be anxious" in both Matthew 6 and Philippians 4 can mean anxious preoccupation, but it can also mean proper concern for others. Paul uses it positively in the same letter, of Timothy, who will be "genuinely concerned" for the Philippians (Philippians 2:20). The note on [Philippians 4](/study/bible/philippians/4) says that in verse 6 it means "the anxious care that divides the mind," and then adds a sentence that changes how the whole verse reads: "Paul's command is not a demand to feel nothing but a direction: turn the worry into prayer."

And the phrase "little faith" is not a dismissal. The disciples Jesus calls by that name are the ones he goes on teaching, rescuing from storms, and feeding. The note on Matthew 6 says it well: "the one he calls ‘of little faith’ he never abandons." It also warns teachers directly: "Above all, avoid using ‘do not worry’ as a rebuke to people suffering from anxiety disorders or depression, as if their illness were simply a lack of faith."

## Two Kinds of Anxiety

What Scripture holds together, and what the church has often pulled apart, is that a human being is one creature made of dust and breath. That means anxiety can come from two directions at once, and the help each needs is different.

There is anxiety as temptation. This is the mind reaching for control it doesn't have, rehearsing tomorrow's disasters because it does not trust anyone else to be awake for them. It is the worry Jesus addresses, and Scripture's answer is to name the false master, to bring the need to the Father by name, and to take up the day's trouble and not tomorrow's: "Sufficient for the day is its own trouble" (Matthew 6:34). This kind of anxiety responds, slowly, to trust learned in practice. It is part of every Christian's life, and confessing it is not shameful.

There is also anxiety as affliction. Here the body's alarm rings with no fire in the room, or keeps ringing long after the fire is out. The heart races, breath shortens, sleep goes, and a sense of dread settles over the day that no argument can lift. The help page describes it with care: "your body has an alarm built to protect you, and in anxiety it rings when there's no fire, or keeps ringing after the fire is out." A person in that condition is not refusing to trust God any more than a person with a broken leg is refusing to walk. Telling them to have more faith is like telling the man with the broken leg to try harder. It adds guilt to the injury and does nothing for the bone.

The two kinds often travel together, and part of wisdom is learning which one you are facing on a given night. Worry that is mostly about control usually loosens when you name what you are clutching and hand it over. Anxiety that is mostly affliction does not respond to argument at all, and it needs sleep, food, time, a doctor, a counselor, and people who will stay. Most anxious people need some of both. The mistake is to treat the second as if it were only the first.

## The Anxious Saints

The strongest answer to the claim that anxiety proves weak faith is the life of Jesus himself. On the night before he died, Mark says that he "began to be greatly distressed and troubled. And he said to them, 'My soul is very sorrowful, even to death'" (Mark 14:33-34). The note on [Mark 14](/study/bible/mark/14) adds that he spoke "in words drawn from Psalms 42 and 43," the psalms of a soul cast down and disturbed. Luke reports that in his agony "his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground" (Luke 22:44), though some early manuscripts lack that verse. Whatever else Gethsemane teaches, it teaches that distress in body and soul is not itself sin. The letter to the Hebrews draws the conclusion: "For we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15).

Paul is the second witness, and he is the more surprising one, because he wrote "do not be anxious about anything." Listing the hardships of his ministry to the Corinthians, after the beatings and shipwrecks he adds this: "And, apart from other things, there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches" (2 Corinthians 11:28). The word there is the same family as the one in Philippians 4. He told the same church that when he came to Troas and did not find Titus, "my spirit was not at rest" (2 Corinthians 2:13), and he left a fruitful opportunity to go and look for him. The apostle who commanded the Philippians to pray instead of worrying was not a man who felt no worry. He was a man who knew where to take it.

The psalms are the third witness. They do not edit the fear out. "When I am afraid, I put my trust in you" (Psalm 56:3) assumes the fear is there. "When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul" (Psalm 94:19) admits the cares before it names the comfort. The church has kept these prayers for nearly three thousand years because anxious people needed them, and God gave them so that anxious people would have something to say.

The history of the church adds witnesses of its own. Martin Luther spoke throughout his life of his *Anfechtungen*, assaults of terror and spiritual dread that came on him again and again, long after he had grasped the gospel of grace that freed others. They did not mean his faith was weak. They were, as he understood them, part of the fight in which faith is exercised.

## What We Did

The church has often been unkind to anxious people, and usually not out of malice. We wanted peace to be visible, so we treated calm as a sign of maturity and anxiety as a lack of it. Anxious believers learned to perform serenity on Sunday and hide the rest. We reached for a verse because it was faster than sitting beside someone whose fear unsettled us. The Matthew 6 note records the critics of the harsher reading, "among them many Christian psychologists and psychiatrists," who "answer that this reading adds guilt to suffering, ignores the bodily and medical causes of anxiety disorders, and has driven people away from help." They are right, and pastors, myself among them, have been slow to listen.

We have also been suspicious of medicine in a way we would never be about any other part of the body. A church that would pray for a broken arm and drive the person to the hospital will sometimes pray for an anxious mind and tell the person to stay away from the doctor. Christians have long received medicine as one of God's ordinary gifts; Paul's companion was "Luke the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14). Whether a given person should take a given medication is a question for that person and a doctor, not for this essay, and not for the pulpit. But taking it is not faithlessness, and the deacon with his morning pill has nothing to hide.

The skeptic says religion is a sedative for frightened people. Some religion has been used that way, and it earned the charge. The faith of the Bible is a poor sedative. It keeps Gethsemane in its story and the anxious psalms in its prayer book, and it does not promise that faithful people will never be afraid.

## What Trust Looks Like

Read in its setting, Philippians 4:6-7 is not a sentence passed on the anxious. It is an invitation with a promise attached. Paul does not say, "Stop feeling this." He says to bring "everything" to God, "by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving." Then the promise: "And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 4:7). The note on Philippians 4 is careful about what that promise is: "The promise is not that every request will be granted as asked, but that the peace of God will guard the heart and mind in Christ Jesus." A guard stands at the door while the trouble is still outside. The verse does not promise that the trouble will leave.

Trust, then, is not the absence of fear. It is what you do with the fear. Sometimes it looks like naming the worry and handing it over in prayer, and finding that the grip loosens. Sometimes it looks like praying the same short prayer twenty times in one night. And sometimes it looks like making the appointment, taking the medicine, telling one friend, and going to bed at the same time every night, because God works through ordinary means and a body that is cared for is easier to pray in. Elijah, worn out and afraid under the broom tree, was given sleep and food twice before he was given a word (1 Kings 19:5-8). God's order of care has not changed.

## If It Is You

You may have come to this essay hoping to be told your anxiety is not your fault. Part of it may not be, and part of it may be tangled with real fears that need real trust. You don't have to sort that out tonight. The help page suggests a place to start: "Tonight, put the worries on paper and leave the list by your bed; you don't have to solve them before morning." Bring the list to God by name, as Philippians 4 says. Then sleep if you can.

If the worry has lasted for weeks, or if it is taking your sleep, your work, or your joy, the page is plain: call your doctor or a licensed counselor this week. A doctor can look for physical causes and talk with you about treatment; a counselor can help with the habits of the mind that keep the loop running. Going is not a sign that your faith failed. It is the same faith, trusting God to work through the people and means he has given.

And if your fear has become thoughts of not wanting to be alive, please call or text 988 tonight. You don't have to be in immediate danger to call. It is there for nights like this one.

## The Disciple Who Fell Asleep

In Gethsemane, Jesus took Peter, James and John a little further into the garden than the others and asked them, "Remain here and watch" (Mark 14:34). He wanted company. Even the Son of God, in the hour of his deepest distress, did not want to be alone with it. The three fell asleep. He came back and found them sleeping, and went back to pray, and came back again.

Years later, one of those three wrote a letter to Christians scattered across Asia Minor who had good reason to be afraid. Peter, the disciple who could not keep his eyes open while his Lord sweated in the dark, told them what to do with their fear. He did not tell them to stop feeling it. He told them where to put it, and why they could: "casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you" (1 Peter 5:7). He had learned it from someone who had been anxious himself and had never stopped caring for the friends who failed him.

The young mother may still be awake tonight. The student may have another attack in chapel. The deacon will take his pill in the morning. None of that is the end of their faith. It may be the place where they learn what Peter learned, that the God who invites anxious people to cast their cares on him was never surprised that they had cares to cast.

*"Casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you."* (1 Peter 5:7)

*"When the cares of my heart are many, your consolations cheer my soul."* (Psalm 94:19)
